title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
The core failure here is a system trained on copyrighted material without the rights holders' authorisation. Udio deployed an AI music generation tool that, according to allegations from multiple major labels and independent artists, used protected recordings as training data. This is a training-data sourcing failure, occurring before deployment, where the inputs used to build the model were not cleared for that use. A rights-clearance check at the data-curation stage, before training began, is where this would have been caught.

The legal landscape around the incident is fragmented. Universal Music Group settled and moved toward a licensing partnership. Warner Music Group did the same. Sony Music filed a separate lawsuit asserting over 30,000 recordings were used without permission, and a class action by independent artists survived a dismissal attempt and was transferred to a new jurisdiction. The settlements are not admissions of liability, the lawsuits are allegations and not verdicts, and what training data Udio actually used is not established by any of these proceedings as reported.

What is established is that deploying a generative AI system trained on commercially released music, without prior licensing agreements, created legal exposure across the entire music industry simultaneously. The subsequent pivot to a licensed platform suggests the original deployment operated outside the conditions that would have made it legally sustainable.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, reaching licensing agreements to end their dispute over copyright infringement. UMG had accused Udio of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence model, including The Temptations' hit "My Girl." Under the settlement, Udio will launch a new platform next year that uses only authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs. The financial terms were not disclosed.

This settlement marks Udio's first licensing agreement with a major music label and represents a shift toward collaboration between AI companies and the music industry. UMG's CEO stated the agreements show their commitment to supporting artists while embracing new technology and creating new revenue streams. Udio's founder expressed enthusiasm about working with UMG to develop tools that empower both artists and fans. Artists who participate in the new platform will receive compensation, though specific details were not provided.
